sentences.text: She came up on the Monday and there was something wrong with her off fore.
Duarte saw it from the window because he was awake, because he was always awake, and because at the top of the hill you have a long time to fill between eight and ten.
She came round the bend and she was not walking wrong exactly — she was walking short.
A shortened step on the right, and a pause at the top of it, of the kind you would notice in an animal you had watched for years and in no other circumstance.
She did the tannery row and the square and the terrace at about the usual time.
She got to the top at twenty to one in the morning.

Duarte went to school on the Tuesday having had about four hours and spent the whole of the bus journey with his forehead against the window, and got seven out of twenty in a maths test he had actually revised for.

Duarte knows the time because he had been lying in the dark for four hours by then in a state he had never been in before, which was not being unable to sleep so much as sleep simply not having arrived in the room.
There is a difference and anybody who has had a bad week knows it.
Tuesday she got there at ten past one.
Wednesday she did not get there at all.
That was the worst of it and it was not the tiredness.
He had been tired before.

What Wednesday night had in it was the other thing — the specific experience of lying in a bed, in the correct position, with the light off, at the correct hour, and finding that the room simply did not contain the material.
It is not the same as insomnia and Duarte has been careful about that distinction his whole life, because he has since had ordinary insomnia and it is nothing like it.
Insomnia is a mind that will not stop.
This was a mind perfectly willing to stop and nothing there to stop into.

He heard her turn back at the terrace — the hooves stopping, the long pause, and then the hooves going away down again — and he lay in his bed at the top of Casal do Meio and stared at a ceiling he could not see until the light came up behind the ridge at about six.
On Thursday morning there were four households at the top of that hill in a state that the rest of the village found extremely funny for about a day and then stopped finding funny.
The stopping was quite sudden and it happened at the shop.

Senhora Aurora came down on the Thursday for bread, which she did every day, and she stood at the counter and could not remember what she had come for, and stood there working at it in front of five people for the better part of a minute.
She was eighty-one and there was nothing whatsoever wrong with her memory.
Everybody in that shop knew it.
And by that afternoon the joke about the top of the hill had gone out of circulation and did not come back for years.
